title: What’s Behind the Violence in Pakistan-Administered Kashmir
gist: Two months of unrest in Pakistan-administered Kashmir have killed at least 40 people and exposed a governance-legitimacy crisis that Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, close to army chief Asim Munir, publicly called a collapsed system; Kugelman argues Islamabad wants it resolved fast so the world watches its Iran-war mediation instead. The brief also flags Sheikh Hasina's pledged December return to Bangladesh, an India and Pakistan carve-out from the new U.S. $20,000 visa bond, and the first armed challenge to the Taliban in nearly five years.

insights.claim: Political unrest in Pakistan-administered Kashmir has run for two months and turned deadly during a three-phase local election running July 27 to Aug. 10, 2026.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: An election calendar overlapping with lethal crackdowns is a recipe for prolonged instability in a nuclear-armed state — watch for escalation through Aug. 10.
insights.quote: The escalation coincided with local elections, which run from July 27 to Aug. 10 in a three-phase process.

insights.claim: At least 40 people have been killed in Pakistan-administered Kashmir since June, with the BBC reporting families who say relatives were shot dead while protesting.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: A confirmed body count converts a local dispute into an international human-rights story that constrains Islamabad's diplomatic positioning.
insights.quote: Death toll estimates vary, but reports suggest at least 40 people have been killed since June.

insights.claim: Authorities cut the internet in the region in June, and the resulting information vacuum was filled by government critics posting fake massacre videos — a case study in how blackouts generate rather than suppress disinformation.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Internet shutdowns as a control tool reliably backfire into credibility loss; treat blackout news as a signal the official narrative is losing.
insights.quote: In an apparent attempt to exaggerate the crisis, government critics posted fake videos depicting massacres on the streets of Kashmir.
insights.locator: Making sense of the simmering crisis

insights.claim: The Joint Awami Action Committee began in 2023 as a cost-of-living movement over food and energy prices before escalating to constitutional demands, showing how economic grievance movements mutate into political ones.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Cost-of-living protest groups in fragile states are leading indicators of constitutional confrontation 18-24 months later.
insights.quote: At the center of the crisis is the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a group formed in 2023 that initially focused its demands on high food and energy prices.
insights.locator: At the center of the crisis

insights.claim: The specific trigger was the JAAC's demand to scrap a constitutional clause reserving 12 legislature seats for refugees from India-administered Kashmir, and rejection by both the regional government and the supreme court hardened the standoff.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: With the demand denied through both political and judicial channels, the remaining escalation path is street confrontation — low odds of near-term de-escalation.
insights.quote: The JAAC argues that since these refugees don’t live in Azad Jammu and Kashmir, Pakistani politicians are exploiting the seats for their own ends.
insights.locator: At the center of the crisis

insights.claim: Protesters have widened their platform beyond constitutional reform to health care and cheaper electricity, so the movement now has demands no single legal fix can satisfy.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Broadened demands make settlement harder and raise the odds of a repressive rather than negotiated outcome.
insights.quote: the JAAC and other protesters have vowed to push on, asserting their fight is about broader demands such as better health care and cheaper electricity, not just constitutional reform.

insights.claim: Kashmir is the latest node in a nationwide pattern of anti-governance protest that already runs through Balochistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Imran Khan's imprisonment, and claims of a rigged 2024 election.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Treat Pakistani unrest as a single systemic risk factor rather than a sequence of local flare-ups when pricing country risk.
insights.quote: Kashmir is the latest ground zero for protests against poor governance in Pakistan.
insights.locator: Kashmir is the latest ground zero

insights.claim: A nationwide protest movement of the kind that toppled governments elsewhere in South Asia is unlikely in Pakistan because social divisions and a repressive environment cap mass-mobilization capacity.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Cuts against the 'Pakistan is next' narrative — the base case is chronic instability without regime change, a different risk profile than abrupt transition.
insights.quote: But that’s unlikely given its social divisions and a repressive political environment that limits the capacity for mass mobilizations.
insights.locator: If these disparate movements managed to come together

insights.claim: Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi publicly said Pakistan's governance system has collapsed and lacks capacity to address the country's problems — an admission whose weight comes from Naqvi's closeness to army chief Asim Munir.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: When the military's proxy voice concedes systemic failure, structural reform or a power reshuffle becomes materially more likely — a key watch item for Pakistan risk.
insights.quote: Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said the governance system has “collapsed” and lacks capacity to address the country’s problems.
insights.locator: Pakistani minister says system is broken

insights.claim: Analysts believe the likely target of Naqvi's reform agenda is devolving power and resources from provincial governments to local authorities, completing what the 2010 constitutional amendment left unfinished.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Local-tier devolution would reshape where fiscal spending and patronage flow in Pakistan — relevant to provincial debt and infrastructure exposure.
insights.quote: Pakistani analysts familiar with the government’s thinking believe that one likely target is the devolution of power and resources from provincial governments to local authorities.
insights.locator: It’s unclear what specific reforms Naqvi

insights.claim: Islamabad's incentive to settle Kashmir quickly is reputational: it wants global attention on its mediation in the Iran war, not on its heavy-handed tactics at home.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Pakistan's diplomatic ambitions in the Iran war give outside powers real leverage over its domestic conduct — a channel for de-escalation pressure.
insights.quote: It wants the world to focus on Islamabad’s mediation efforts in the Iran war, not its heavy-handed tactics in Kashmir.
insights.locator: Still, Pakistan’s national leadership has a strong incentive

insights.claim: Sheikh Hasina, sentenced to death in absentia last November for crimes against humanity, reiterated from exile in India that she will return to Bangladesh in December and surrender to legal authorities.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: A December return would be a destabilizing event for Bangladesh political risk — a dated catalyst for anyone with taka or Bangladeshi credit exposure.
insights.quote: She reiterated her pledge to return to Bangladesh in December and turn herself in to legal authorities.

insights.claim: The United Nations estimates as many as 1,400 people may have died in the crackdowns that preceded Hasina's 2024 flight, the basis for her in-absentia death sentence.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: The scale of the underlying charges makes any negotiated return or amnesty politically impossible in Dhaka.
insights.quote: According to the United Nations, as many as 1,400 people may have died during the protests.
insights.locator: Last November, Hasina—who has remained in India

insights.claim: India conspicuously distanced itself from Hasina's New Delhi event because it is trying to reset ties with Bangladesh's new BNP-led government, a bitter rival of her Awami League.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: New Delhi is trading a legacy ally for working relations with Dhaka's incumbents — a sign India prioritizes regional trade and border stability over personal loyalties.
insights.quote: India had a strong interest in signaling that it was not endorsing Hasina’s event or trying to provide her with a platform.
insights.locator: As a result, India had a strong interest

insights.claim: A U.S. policy effective Aug. 1, 2026 can require refundable deposits of up to $20,000 for B-1 and B-2 visas from citizens of 50 countries, with India and Pakistan exempted while Bangladesh and Nepal are included.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: A five-figure travel bond is a de facto tariff on people flows — negative for Bangladeshi and Nepali business travel and U.S.-bound tourism from those markets.
insights.quote: a policy that went into effect on Aug. 1 and is intended to reduce overstays.
insights.locator: India and Pakistan exempted from new U.S. visa bond

insights.claim: The exemption pattern cannot be explained by bilateral warmth, since Bangladesh and Pakistan have both logged recent achievements with Washington while U.S.-India ties have sputtered, suggesting opaque or bureaucratic criteria.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Unpredictable U.S. visa policy adds a hard-to-hedge compliance variable for firms staffing U.S. operations from South Asia.
insights.quote: It’s not a matter of doing a favor for countries on good terms with U.S. President Donald Trump: Bangladesh and Pakistan have each logged bilateral achievements with the United States in recent months, while U.S.-India ties have sputtered.

themes.theme: First armed challenge to the Taliban

insights.claim: Sami Sadat's Afghanistan United Front, previously a political opposition group, claimed an armed strike on the Taliban's main police headquarters in Kandahar — the first organized armed resistance in nearly five years of Taliban rule.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: A credible insurgency reopening in Afghanistan is a regional risk repricing event — watch Pakistan border security and any Western backing signals.
insights.quote: On Monday, a post on its official X account said that the group had struck the Taliban’s main police headquarters in Kandahar, Afghanistan.

insights.claim: The AUF's prospects are weak because it requires the type of external backing anti-Taliban factions enjoyed before 2001, and the world has effectively moved on from Afghanistan.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Low probability the AUF becomes a strategic threat absent a sponsor — treat as headline risk rather than a regime-change scenario.
insights.quote: The Taliban remain a formidable force; to become stronger, the AUF will need the type of external backing that anti-Taliban factions enjoyed before 2001.
insights.locator: Sadat, who has been based in northern Virginia

insights.claim: War fatigue is a binding constraint on any Afghan insurgency: Sadat claims he can mobilize tens of thousands of recruits, but many Afghans do not want another war.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Popular exhaustion caps insurgency scale independently of funding — a useful discount to apply to any exile group's mobilization claims.
insights.quote: And while Sadat has spoken of the capacity to quickly mobilize tens of thousands of recruits, many Afghans don’t want another war.
insights.locator: With the world essentially moving on
